title: AGEoTD: Prediction of the chronological age of a person in different biological trace materials
summary:
The examination of DNA, the storehouse of genetic information, plays an essential role in forensic casework.  The main task here is to assign biological traces. However, DNA also contains other valuable information and can, for example, provide information about the age of the person who left the trace. Estimating the age of the person who caused the trace can help to narrow down the circle of possible persons if, for example, no assignment is possible due to a lack of suspects or persons involved. However, the investigated trace material has a direct influence on the estimation of the age, since the biological origin (e.g. blood, saliva, sperm) as well as the DNA quantity and DNA quality play a role. 
The study will create, test, and validate mathematical models for estimating age. While the base sequence of DNA within an individual is identical in all cells, chemical modification of nucleic acids (e.g. DNA methylation), among others, achieves cell-specific behavior (e.g. tissue-specific morphological properties, secretion of hormones). Such specific DNA methylation patterns can be used, for example, to determine cell type, but also to allow age estimation. For this purpose, age-dependent markers have been identified in the past (or are still being found), which can be used to enable age estimation with the help of a mathematical model. However, the material analyzed plays a major role in this process, as the change in DNA methylation with age occurs at different rates in different biomaterials. Therefore, it is not possible to use a model created on the basis of blood samples for saliva samples as well, as this may lead to erroneous estimates. 
Known and newly identified markers (= sites in the genome, with chemical modification), which change with age, are to be used to improve the estimation of age. For this purpose, mathematical models for estimating age will be created for body fluids and tissue types. Additional investigation of markers that determine cell type will further optimize the study. Above all, the examination of crime scene traces is to be recreated and verified (validated) by creating artificial traces. This will allow factors such as DNA quality and quantity to be incorporated into the mathematical models.
For the study presented, tests will be conducted on DNA from volunteer participants from blood, saliva, buccal mucosal scrapings, vaginal fluid, seminal fluid, menstrual blood, nasal secretions, skin cells (dander), and hair. In addition, artificial mixed traces are created with the help of these materials in order to imitate crime scene traces (including different storage periods).
